section.heading: 1.5 Solution Sets of Linear Systems
section.paragraph: Solution sets of linear systems are important objects of study in linear algebra. They will appear later in several different contexts. This section uses vector notation to give explicit and geometric descriptions of such solution sets.
section.heading: Homogeneous Linear Systems
section.paragraph: A system of linear equations is said to be homogeneous if it can be written in the form $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ , where $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix and $$0$$ is the zero vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ . Such a system $$A \mathbf{x} = 0$$ always has at least one solution, namely $$\mathbf{x} = 0$$ (the zero vector in $$\left. \mathbb{R}^{n} \right)$$ . This zero solution is usually called the trivial solution. For a given equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0 \text{,}$$ the important question is whether there exists a nontrivial solution, that is, a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ that satisfies $$A\mathbf{x} = 0.$$ The Existence and Uniqueness Theorem in Section 1.2 (Theorem 2) leads immediately to the following fact.

note.paragraph: The homogeneous equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has a nontrivial solution if and only if the equation has at least one free variable.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Determine if the following homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution. Then describe the solution set.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be the matrix of coefficients of the system and row reduce the augmented matrix $$\lbrack A 0\rbrack$$ to echelon form:

Since $$x_{3}$$ is a free variable, $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has nontrivial solutions (one for each nonzero choice of $$x_{3}$$ ). To describe the solution set, continue the row reduction of $$\lbrack A 0\rbrack$$ to reduced echelon form:

Solve for the basic variables $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ and obtain $$x_{1} = \frac{4}{3}x_{3}$$ , $$x_{2} = 0$$ , with $$x_{3}$$ free. As a vector, the general solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has the form

$$\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{4}{3} x_{3} \\ 0 \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} = x_{3} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{4}{3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = x_{3} \mathbf{v} , \text{where} \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{4}{3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Here $$x_{3}$$ is factored out of the expression for the general solution vector. This shows that every solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ in this case is a scalar multiple of $$\mathbf{v}$$ . The trivial solution is obtained by choosing $$x_{3} = 0.$$ Geometrically, the solution set is a line through $$0$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . See Figure 1.

example.paragraph: Click here for an Interactive version of Figure 1

section.paragraph: Notice that a nontrivial solution $$\mathbf{x}$$ can have some zero entries so long as not all of its entries are zero.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: A single linear equation can be treated as a very simple system of equations. Describe all solutions of the homogeneous “system”
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: There is no need for matrix notation. Solve for the basic variable $$x_{1}$$ in terms of the free variables. The general solution is $$x_{1} = .3x_{2} + .2x_{3}$$ , with $$x_{2}$$ and $$x_{3}$$ free. As a vector, the general solution is

$$\textbf{x} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.3 x_{2} + .2 x_{2} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.3 x_{2} \\ x_{2} \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.2 x 3 \\ 0 \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & x_{2} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. + x_{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. ( \text{with} x_{2} , x_{ \text{3} } \text{free} ) & & \begin{matrix} & \overset{ \uparrow}{ \textbf{u}} & & \end{matrix} \overset{ \uparrow}{ \textbf{v}}$$

This calculation shows that every solution of (1) is a linear combination of the vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ , shown in (2). That is, the solution set is $$\text{Span} \{\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v}\}$$ . Since neither $$\mathbf{u}$$ nor $$\mathbf{v}$$ is a scalar multiple of the other, the solution set is a plane through the origin. See Figure 2.

image.alt: A graph shows a tilted parallelogram with one vertex resting on the origin of the three-dimensional plane.

section.paragraph: Examples 1 and 2, along with the exercises, illustrate the fact that the solution set of a homogeneous equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ can always be expressed explicitly as $$\text{Span\{} \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \text{\}}$$ for suitable vectors $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ . If the only solution is the zero vector, then the solution set is $$\text{Span\{} \textbf{0} \text{\}}$$ . If the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has only one free variable, the solution set is a line through the origin, as in Figure 1. A plane through the origin, as in Figure 2, provides a good mental image for the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ when there are two or more free variables. Note, however, that a similar figure can be used to visualize $$\text{Span} \text{\{} \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{\}}$$ even when $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ do not arise as solutions of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0.$$ See Figure 11 in Section 1.3.
section.heading: Parametric Vector Form
section.paragraph: The original equation (1) for the plane in Example 2 is an implicit description of the plane. Solving this equation amounts to finding an explicit description of the plane as the set spanned by $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ . Equation (2) is called a parametric vector equation of the plane. Sometimes such an equation is written as

to emphasize that the parameters vary over all real numbers. In Example 1, the equation $$\mathbf{x} = x_{3}\mathbf{v}$$ (with $$x_{3}$$ free), or $$\mathbf{x} = t\mathbf{v}$$ (with $$t$$ in $$\mathbb{R}$$ ), is a parametric vector equation of a line. Whenever a solution set is described explicitly with vectors as in Examples 1 and 2, we say that the solution is in parametric vector form.
section.heading: Solutions of Nonhomogeneous Systems
section.paragraph: When a nonhomogeneous linear system has many solutions, the general solution can be written in parametric vector form as one vector plus an arbitrary linear combination of vectors that satisfy the corresponding homogeneous system.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Describe all solutions of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ , where
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 & - 4 \\ - 3 & - 2 & 4 \\ 6 & 1 & - 8 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ - 1 \\ - 4 \end{bmatrix}$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Here $$A$$ is the matrix of coefficients from Example 1. Row operations on $$\lbrack A \mathbf{b}\rbrack$$ produce
Thus $$x_{1} = - 1 + \frac{4}{3}x^{3}$$ , $$x_{2} = 2$$ , and $$x_{3}$$ is free. As a vector, the general solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ has the form

$$\text{x} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 + \frac{4}{3} x_{3} \\ 2 \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. & + & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\frac{4}{3} x_{3} \\ 0 \\ x_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. & + & x_{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & & & & & & & & & & \overset{\uparrow}{ \text{p} } & & \overset{\uparrow}{ \text{v} }$$
The equation $$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} + x_{3}\mathbf{v}$$ , or, writing $$t$$ as a general parameter,
$$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v} \left(\right. t \text{in} \mathbb{R} \left.\right)$$
describes the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ in parametric vector form. Recall from Example 1 that the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ has the parametric vector equation
$$\mathbf{x} = t \mathbf{v} \left(\right. t \text{in} \mathbb{R} \left.\right)$$

[with the same $$\mathbf{v}$$ that appears in (3)]. Thus the solutions of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ are obtained by adding the vector $$\mathbf{p}$$ to the solutions of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ . The vector $$\mathbf{p}$$ itself is just one particular solution of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ [corresponding to $$t = 0$$ in (3)].

section.paragraph: To describe the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ geometrically, we can think of vector addition as a translation. Given $$\mathbf{v}$$ and $$\mathbf{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ or $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , the effect of adding $$\mathbf{p}$$ to $$\mathbf{v}$$ is to move $$\mathbf{v}$$ in a direction parallel to the line through $$\mathbf{p}$$ and $$0$$ . We say that $$\mathbf{v}$$ is translated by $$p$$ to $$\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{p}$$ . See Figure 3. If each point on a line $$L$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ or $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ is translated by a vector $$\mathbf{p}$$ , the result is a line parallel to $$L$$ . See Figure 4.

Suppose $$L$$ is the line through $$0$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ , described by equation (4). Adding $$\mathbf{p}$$ to each point on $$L$$ produces the translated line described by equation (3). Note that $$\mathbf{p}$$ is on the line in equation (3). We call (3) the equation of the line through $$p$$ parallel to $$v$$ . Thus the solution set of $$A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ is a line through $$\mathbf{p}$$ parallel to the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ . Figure 5 illustrates this case.

image.alt: A figure shows two slanted parallel lines on a coordinate plane.

figure.caption: Figure 5 Parallel solution sets of Ax=b and Ax=0﻿

section.paragraph: Click here for an Interactive version of Figure 5

The relation between the solution sets of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ and $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ shown in Figure 5 generalizes to any consistent equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ , although the solution set will be larger than a line when there are several free variables. The following theorem gives the precise statement. See Exercise 37 at the end of this section for a proof.

note.title: Theorem 6
note.heading: Theorem 6
note.paragraph: Suppose the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ is consistent for some given $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and let $$\mathbf{p}$$ be a solution. Then the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ is the set of all vectors of the form $$\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}_{h}$$ , where $$\mathbf{v}_{h}$$ is any solution of the homogeneous equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ .

section.paragraph: Theorem 6 says that if $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ has a solution, then the solution set is obtained by translating the solution set of $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ , using any particular solution $$\mathbf{p}$$ of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ for the translation. Figure 6 illustrates the case in which there are two free variables. Even when $$n > 3$$ , our mental image of the solution set of a consistent system $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ (with $$\mathbf{b} \neq 0$$ ) is either a single nonzero point or a line or plane not passing through the origin.

image.alt: A figure shows two rectangular planes lying on the three-dimensional plane stacked on each other.

section.paragraph: Warning: Theorem 6 and Figure 6 apply only to an equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ that has at least one nonzero solution $$\mathbf{p}$$ . When $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ has no solution, the solution set is empty.
The following algorithm outlines the calculations shown in Examples 1, 2, and 3.

note.heading: Writing a Solution Set (of a Consistent System) in Parametric Vector Form

list.item: Row reduce the augmented matrix to reduced echelon form.
Express each basic variable in terms of any free variables appearing in an equation.
Write a typical solution $$\mathbf{x}$$ as a vector whose entries depend on the free variables, if any.
Decompose $$\mathbf{x}$$ into a linear combination of vectors (with numeric entries) using the free variables as parameters.

note.title: Reasonable Answers
note.heading: Reasonable Answers
note.paragraph: To verify that the solutions you found are indeed solutions to the homogeneous equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ , simply multiply the matrix by each vector in your solution and check that the result is the zero vector. For example, if $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 2} & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & {- 1} & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix},$$ and you found the homogeneous solutions to be $$x_{3}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack + x_{4}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 8} \\ {- 3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ check $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 2} & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & {- 1} & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 2} & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & {- 1} & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 8} \\ {- 3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$ Then $$A\left( {x_{3}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack + x_{4}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 8} \\ {- 3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack} \right) = x_{3}A\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack + x_{4}A\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 8} \\ {- 3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ which is equal to $$x_{3}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_{4}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},$$ as desired.

If you are solving $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ , then you can again verify that you have correct solutions by multiplying the matrix by each vector in your solutions. The product of $$A$$ with the first vector (the one that is not part of the solution to the homogeneous equation) should be $$\mathbf{b}$$ . The product of $$A$$ with the remaining vectors (the ones that are part of the solution to the homogeneous equation) should of course be $$0$$ .

For example, to verify that $$\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + x_{3}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack + x_{4}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 8} \\ {- 3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ are solutions to $$A\mathbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ 13 \\ 8 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ check $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 2} & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & {- 1} & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ 13 \\ 8 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and use the calculations from above. Notice $$A\left( {\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + x_{3}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack + x_{4}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 8} \\ {- 3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack} \right) = A\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + x_{3}A\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack + x_{4}A\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 8} \\ {- 3} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack \text{,}$$ which is equal to $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ 13 \\ 8 \end{array} \right\rbrack + x_{3}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_{4}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ 13 \\ 8 \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ as desired.
